Spoil
SPOIL
n. and v. (rendering Hebrew shālāl, baz, and Greek skula, apekduomai)
From Old French espoillier, from Latin spoliare, to strip — from spolium, the hide stripped from an animal and thence the armour stripped from a defeated enemy. The original sense is stripping, and both the Hebrew shālāl and the Greek skula keep it: spoil is what is taken off the vanquished. The modern English sense of to ruin is a later development from the same stripping figure.

Biblical Definition

Spoil is what victory takes, and Scripture uses it in three ascending senses. Historically, it is plunder: at the Exodus “they spoiled the Egyptians” (Exo 12:36), the LORD having given the people favour so that the goods of their oppressors went out with them — back wages for four centuries of unpaid labour, and the material out of which the tabernacle would later be built. Prophetically, it belongs to the Servant: “he shall divide the spoil with the strong; because he hath poured out his soul unto death” (Isa 53:12), the only conqueror in Scripture who wins the spoil by dying. Doctrinally, Paul brings it to its head at the cross: “having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it” (Col 2:15) — the imagery is a Roman triumph in which the defeated are stripped of their arms and led publicly behind the victor's chariot, and the powers so treated are the spiritual ones that held men under the handwriting of ordinances. The place where the cross looked most like defeat is named by the apostle as the place of the stripping and the parade. Finally, the psalmist takes the figure and applies it to Scripture itself: “I rejoice at thy word, as one that findeth great spoil” (Psa 119:162) — the joy of the soldier who opens a captured tent, applied to a man opening his Bible.

Webster 1828 Definition

That which is taken by force from an enemy; in Scripture the goods of Egypt given to Israel at the Exodus, the portion the dying Servant divides with the strong, the arms stripped from principalities and powers at the cross, and the psalmist's figure for the joy of finding God's word.

expand to see more

SPOIL, v.t. 1. To plunder; to strip by violence; to rob. They spoiled the Egyptians. Exod. 12.

2. To seize by violence; to take by force. Lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit. Col. 2.

3. To corrupt; to cause to decay and perish; whence the modern common use of the word.

4. SPOIL, n. That which is taken from others by violence; pillage; plunder; particularly the arms and armor stripped from a vanquished enemy.

5. To divide the spoil; to share the fruits of a victory. He shall divide the spoil with the strong. Isa. 53.

Key Scripture

Exodus 12:36 — "And the LORD gave the people favour in the sight of the Egyptians, so that they lent unto them such things as they required. And they spoiled the Egyptians."

Isaiah 53:12 — "Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong; because he hath poured out his soul unto death: and he was numbered with the transgressors; and he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors."

Luke 11:22 — "But when a stronger than he shall come upon him, and overcome him, he taketh from him all his armour wherein he trusted, and divideth his spoils."

Psalm 119:162 — "I rejoice at thy word, as one that findeth great spoil."

Modern Corruption

The spoiling of the Egyptians is charged as divinely sanctioned theft, and Col 2:15 is quietly reduced to a metaphor for encouragement — when the first was restitution and the second is the objective defeat of real powers.

expand to see more

The objection to Exo 12:36 is old and is usually pressed as a moral scandal: God, it is said, commanded His people to borrow with no intention of returning. The text does not say that. The Hebrew verb rendered lent means simply to ask or request, and the Egyptians gave what was asked because the LORD gave the people favour in their sight. More to the point, Israel had built store cities for four hundred years without wages, and the law God would shortly give commands that a freed servant not be sent away empty but furnished liberally out of the flock and the floor. What happened at the Exodus is the pattern of that very law applied to a nation. The goods were not stolen; they were the severance owed to emancipated slaves, and much of it was afterward given back to God for the making of the tabernacle.

Col 2:15 suffers a gentler loss. It is often read as a general assurance that Christians should feel confident, with the principalities and powers treated as figures of speech for difficulty or fear. Paul means something objective and public. There were real rulers and authorities holding real claims over men through the law's just condemnation; the handwriting of ordinances that was against us was nailed to the cross, and with the claim cancelled the claimants were disarmed. That is why the passage begins with a legal document and ends with a triumph. The pastoral force follows from the fact, not from a mood: because the powers have actually been stripped, the Colossians need not submit to ordinances, philosophy, angel worship, or the judgment of anyone in respect of meat, drink, or holy days.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shālāl is booty or plunder; baz is spoil taken in a raid. Greek skula is arms stripped from the slain, and apekduomai, the verb in Col 2:15, means to strip off completely — the same verb used of putting off the old man.

expand to see more

Hebrew shālāl (H7998) — spoil, plunder, booty; the word in Isa 53:12 and in the name Maher-shalal-hash-baz, haste to the spoil (Isa 8:1).

Hebrew baz (H957) — spoil, prey; used of Judah given for a spoil and of the nations that spoiled Israel.

Greek skula (G4661) — arms and armour stripped from a defeated foe; used in Luk 11:22, where the stronger man taketh from him all his armour and divideth his spoils.

Greek apekduomai (G554) — to strip off wholly, to disarm; the verb of Col 2:15, and used again in Col 3:9 of putting off the old man with his deeds.

Greek thriambeuō (G2358) — to lead in triumph; the verb behind triumphing over them, drawn from the Roman triumphal procession.

Usage

"Of plunder in history: they spoiled the Egyptians (Exo 12:36); the spoil of the Midianites divided (Num 31:27)."

"Of the Servant's reward: he shall divide the spoil with the strong (Isa 53:12)."

"Of the cross and of the word: having spoiled principalities and powers (Col 2:15); I rejoice at thy word, as one that findeth great spoil (Psa 119:162)."
